source.title: HINT: Hierarchical Neuron Concept Explainer
source.authors: Andong Wang; Wei-Ning Lee; Xiaojuan Qi

page_placements.theme: What units match, and how interpretable they are, varies with layer depth

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies neuron–concept associations in image-classification CNNs, but it does not test the listed claim versions: it does not audit language-model neuron poles, test the cited InceptionV1 examples, or assess language-model explanations on held-out activations or new text.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own neuron–concept results, including multimodal neurons and concept-classifier results. These are recorded as findings about the broader subject, with versions set to none; they do not measure the specific quantities or behaviors named by V1–V7. Results comparing HINT with other localization methods are not extracted here as they assess localization performance rather than a claim version.
record.test_reason: HINT is a vision-CNN neuron–concept association method. It reports no share of neurons with one main job, no language models, and no analysis of InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or pose. It runs no tool or architecture comparison of interpretable-neuron shares, builds no attribution graphs, and does no held-out or simulation scoring of explanations. Its multimodal-neuron findings (for example, neuron 199 linked to both bird and car in VGG-19) are related observations but do not measure any version's quantity. The 'multimodal' label comes from classifier Shapley scores, not from a test of superposition against a shared feature.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that HINT builds bidirectional neuron–hierarchical-concept associations in a low-cost, scalable way. They say it identifies collaborative and multimodal neurons, shows that CNNs implicitly embed hierarchical concepts, and is validated by WSOL and other applications.
record.recipe_differences: HINT uses saliency-guided hidden-layer regions, trained concept classifiers, and Shapley contribution scores for ImageNet-trained CNNs; it is not the cited language-model neuron-explanation audit or held-out-text scoring procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Concept-classifier F1 for mammal changes by layer, rising from 0.04 on features.10 to around 0.8 on features.30 (R1–R5).

fits_no_version.finding: VGG-19 neuron 199 on features.30 receives high HINT contribution to both bird and car; the authors call them conceptually far apart.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision CNN neurons can be associated with semantically distant concepts by classifier-based attribution.

fits_no_version.finding: VGG-19 neuron 445 contributes most to animal, vertebrate, mammal and carnivore, and also to canine.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single CNN neurons can encode a hierarchy of related concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: Mammal concept-classifier F1 rises from 0.04 (features.10) to about 0.8 (features.30) in VGG-19.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-level concepts become linearly separable in deeper CNN layers.

fits_no_version.finding: On Inception v3 Mixed 6b (768 neurons), 711, 615 and 387 neurons have positive contribution to animal, person and plant respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept contributions are distributed across many neurons, varying with the concept's share of training data.

record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (as stated in the supplied metadata)
record.problems: The results are for image-classification CNNs and WordNet/ImageNet concepts, not language models or neuron poles. HINT's concept hierarchy is predefined; the authors say it cannot handle concepts outside that hierarchy or concepts below the classification-category level. The reported concept associations and classifier/localization checks do not establish the listed language-model audit shares or held-out explanation performance. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the extracted results.
record.rows_left_out: Localization-accuracy comparisons in Tables 1, 2, and S.3–S.6, adversarial-attack and COVID19 applications, and saliency-method comparisons were not extracted: they report localization or application performance, not a result measuring any listed claim version or a more direct neuron–concept finding.

untested.parts: All: no Qwen3-32B pole audit or job-share proportions.
All: no language models, MoE, or scale comparison.
All: no InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis, pose, or recursive generalization.
All: no interpretable-neuron shares by tool or architecture.
All: no attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
All: no test of whether explanations predict firing beyond activating examples.

record.verdict_notes: Vision CNN interpretability method paper; no version is tested. Its 'multimodal neurons' are defined by Shapley scores on linear concept classifiers, not by activation-based polysemanticity analysis, so they cannot be counted for or against V3 or V1. There is a main-text versus supplement discrepancy on the car-wheel response of neuron 199.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole audit and its one-job, two-related-jobs, and not-understood proportions; no comparable language-model audit.
No language models, dense-versus-MoE comparison, or scaling up to trillions of parameters.
No analysis of the cited InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, or recursive generalization.
No estimates of interpretable-neuron shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models or comparison of architecture, regularization, and tools as causes of those shares.
No attribution graphs or comparison against a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
No test of explanations against held-out activating examples or where neurons fire.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: VGG-19

rows.subject: VGG-19
rows.operation_detail: Used HINT to identify a neuron associated with multiple concepts and inspected activation maps.
rows.measure: Reported concept associations and activation-map interpretation
rows.value: The neuron is reported to contribute to both bird and car; the supplementary text says its maps activate the bird head while deactivating car wheels.
rows.locator: Section 4.2; Supplementary Sections E.1 and E.3
rows.note: The main text also says the bird classifier responds to car wheels. The reported association does not test the cited pose explanation or recursive generalization.
rows.check: The main text says the bird classifier detects bird body and car wheels. The supplement says the neuron activates bird head but deactivates car wheels. These are internally inconsistent. The row is a VGG-19 neuron, not InceptionV1, and has no pose analysis, so it cannot bear on V3.

relation.reason: The paper discusses neuron-concept associations in CNNs. It does not test the claim.

tranche.reason: HINT is a vision-CNN neuron-concept method. It does not test or use the claim. Its multimodal-neuron examples (VGG19 neurons 199 and 445) are not InceptionV1 and are not tested for a shared coherent feature, so they don't test V3.

source_check.notes: All five rows match the text. F1 is from classifiers trained on the top-10 responsible neurons per layer (N=10), not a share of neurons with one main job. The paper (2022) predates and does not cite the claim's essay.
